local.levelRationale: NYC still discharges ~18 billion gallons/year of untreated combined sewage through 398 outfalls (CSO), and the city has missed its first two green-infrastructure milestones (1.5% by 2015, 4% by 2020, against a 2030 goal), which argues for 'needs attention.' That is offset by genuinely large, verified nitrogen-specific point-source gains (>58% cut at the four East River WRRFs, ~50%+ cut into Jamaica Bay since 2010) and a harbor-wide dissolved-oxygen record that has been above the NYS 5.0 mg/L standard every summer since the 1990s — real, monitored improvement a small-city groundwater-nitrate problem like Petaluma's does not have an equivalent to.
local.indicator: Combined sewer overflow (CSO) annual discharge volume, paired with wastewater nitrogen loading to receiving waters
local.value: ~18 billion gallons/year of combined sewage discharged citywide through 398 CSO outfalls (~60% of NYC is combined-sewered). Nitrogen: the four East River WRRFs (Wards Island, Hunts Point, Bowery Bay, Tallman Island) cut aggregate nitrogen discharge by >58% after a $1B+ upgrade program; the four Jamaica Bay WRRFs (Jamaica, 26th Ward, Coney Island, Rockaway) cut nitrogen loading to Jamaica Bay from a historic ~54,000 lbs/day to a currently reported ~18,000-20,000 lbs/day.
local.target: Reduce CSO volume by 1.67 billion gallons/year by 2040 and spend $3.5B on green infrastructure by 2045 (2023 CSO Consent Order Modification, DEC Case CO2-20110512-25 modifying CO2-20000107-8). Nitrogen: Long Island Sound TMDL (EPA-approved 2001) requires an aggregate 58.5% reduction in human-generated nitrogen vs. a 1990 baseline; the 2010 Jamaica Bay Nitrogen Consent Agreement targeted ~50% reduction in WRRF nitrogen loading to the bay.
local.context: This is a wastewater-and-CSO story, not an agricultural-runoff story — the sharp structural contrast with Petaluma, where the same dimension is scored on groundwater nitrate near farms and septic systems. NYC's 14 WRRFs and 398 combined-sewer outfalls mean nitrogen and pathogen loading are concentrated at engineered point sources tied to rain events, not diffuse land-based leaching. The policy levers are capital-intensive: WRRF biological nutrient removal retrofits (East River, Jamaica Bay), CSO storage tunnels (Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay), and the green infrastructure program, which the city is currently behind schedule on. Caveat: the citywide 18 BGY figure and the 398-outfall count are the most current published DEP/DEC figures, but a single up-to-date, citywide nitrogen-loading total across all 14 WRRFs (as opposed to per-facility figures of varying vintage) was not found in this search.
local.source: NYSDEC 'New York City CSO Program' page (citing NYC DEP data) and NYC DEP Combined Sewer Overflows page

bronx.value: Hunts Point WRRF (Bronx): biological nitrogen removal retrofit cut nitrogen discharge from ~22,000 lbs/day to ~12,000 lbs/day (~45% reduction), part of the East River WRRF upgrade program.
bronx.note: Year of this specific figure is not stated in the secondary source found (City Limits reporting on the East River/LIS cleanup program); treat as circa the East River WRRF upgrade completion period (2010s), not a fresh 2025/2026 measurement.
bronx.source: City Limits, 'City Expands East River & Long Island Sound Cleanup Effort'

brooklyn.value: 26th Ward WRRF (Brooklyn, serves Jamaica Bay): new carbon-addition facility completed, cutting nitrogen discharge by >3,000 lbs/day (~10% of total Jamaica Bay WRRF loading). Separately, Gowanus Canal (Brooklyn) received an estimated 659 million gallons/year of CSO under its approved Long Term Control Plan baseline.
brooklyn.note: 26th Ward figure is recent per DEP reporting reflected in 2026 search coverage but no publication date was confirmed; Gowanus 659 MGY figure's baseline year is not stated in the source. Owls Head, Red Hook, and Coney Island WRRFs are also in Brooklyn but no nitrogen figures were found for them specifically.
brooklyn.source: NYC DEP program reporting (nitrogen reduction facility) and Waterfront Alliance LTCP coverage

manhattan.value: Wards Island WRRF (administratively Manhattan/Randall's Island, discharges to the Upper East River/Long Island Sound): nitrogen upgrade completed, cutting discharge from 33,000 lbs/day to 17,000 lbs/day (~48% reduction).
manhattan.source: Save the Sound, 'Wards Island Completes Upgrade, Removing Half the Nitrogen in its Waste'

queens.value: Tallman Island WRRF (Queens): $230M upgrade cut nitrogen discharge by >3,500 lbs/day (~1.3 million lbs/year). Bowery Bay (Queens) is also one of the four East River WRRFs; Jamaica and Rockaway WRRFs (Queens) are two of the four Jamaica Bay facilities. Flushing Bay (Queens) is slated for a 28-million-gallon CSO storage tank plus 15 million gallons of in-system storage, still in design/construction as of the 2026 Q1 CSO quarterly report.
queens.note: Tallman Island press-release year not independently confirmed in this pass (URL pattern suggests ~2014); Flushing Bay storage project has no completion year yet — it is under an active alternative-scope modification as of Dec 2025-Mar 2026.
queens.source: NYC DEP press materials (nitrogen reduction) and DEC NYC CSO program page

statenIsland.value: Staten Island is largely separately sewered rather than combined-sewered: the Bluebelt program manages stormwater across ~10,000 acres in 16 watersheds in the southern/eastern part of the island using natural drainage corridors instead of combined sewers, which by design avoids the CSO/nitrogen-shock-load pattern seen elsewhere. The borough's two WRRFs (Oakwood Beach, Port Richmond) were not found to have published nitrogen-loading figures in this search.
statenIsland.note: No borough-wide CSO volume or WRRF nitrogen figure was found for Staten Island specifically (DEP does not appear to publish one, likely because the borough has few/no CSO outfalls); the Bluebelt acreage figure is DEP's own publication, but I could not confirm what share of the island's total land area (~58 sq mi) that 10,000 acres represents from a primary source, so I am not stating a percentage.

local.neighborhoodNote: Jamaica Bay (bordering southeast Brooklyn and southern Queens/the Rockaways) and the Gowanus Canal (Brooklyn) are the sharpest intra-city hot spots: both are enclosed, low-flushing waterbodies where nitrogen loading has historically driven hypoxia and salt-marsh loss, versus open, well-flushed reaches of the East River/Upper Bay where the Harbor Survey shows dissolved oxygen consistently meeting state standards. Source: NYC DEP Jamaica Bay page and Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers timeline (https://www.nyc.gov/site/dep/water/jamaica-bay.page, https://jamaicabayecowatchers.org/about-us/timeline-history-and-accomplishments/).

subIndicators.name: Harbor-wide summer average dissolved oxygen
subIndicators.value: Above the NYS minimum standard of 5.0 mg/L every summer since the 1990s, at open-water sites (surface and bottom), based on a 40-site weekly Harbor Survey run since 1909
subIndicators.source: NYC DEP Harbor Survey Program / NYC Environment & Health Data Portal

subIndicators.name: Green infrastructure milestone compliance
subIndicators.value: City missed both prior 5-year milestones under its Green Infrastructure Grant Program order (1.5% of combined-sewer-area impervious surface managed by 2015; 4% by 2020), against a goal of managing GI on ~8,000 of the ~78,000 impervious acres (10%) by 2030; cumulative GI-attributable CSO reduction reported at 668 million gallons/year as of December 2025
subIndicators.source: Center for an Urban Future / NYC DEP green infrastructure milestone certification

subIndicators.name: Jamaica Bay nitrogen loading trend
subIndicators.value: Reduced from a historic ~54,000 lbs/day to ~18,000-20,000 lbs/day, roughly a 50%+ cut, under the 2010 Nitrogen Consent Agreement ($100M in WRRF nitrogen-control technology + $15M for marsh restoration)
subIndicators.source: The Wave / Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers reporting; NRDC

global.levelRationale: No NYC-specific quantified nitrogen- or phosphorus-footprint study was located, so this level rests on a proxy: nitrogen is one of the planetary boundaries scientists (Steffen et al. 2015, Rockström et al.) consider already transgressed globally at a 'high risk' level via synthetic fertilizer use, and NYC's food supply is entirely import-dependent on that globally overshot system. That directional judgment supports a 'needs attention'-to-'critical' score, but the lack of a city-specific number keeps me from placing it higher with confidence.
global.indicator: NYC's embodied/consumption-based nitrogen footprint via its imported food supply (no verified city-specific study found; scaled from national per-capita averages as an order-of-magnitude proxy)
global.value: Not directly measured for NYC. The U.S. average per-capita nitrogen footprint is reported as roughly 30-41 kg N/person/year (dominated by food production), per the N-Print project (University of Virginia). Applying that national average to NYC's ~8.3M residents implies a rough order-of-magnitude footprint of roughly 250,000-340,000 metric tons N/year — this is an extrapolation from a national figure, not a measured NYC number, and should be treated as illustrative only.
global.target: No NYC-specific target exists. The relevant global anchor is the planetary nitrogen boundary itself: Steffen et al. (2015) put the safe boundary for anthropogenic nitrogen fixation at 62-82 Tg N/year, against actual global fixation estimated at roughly 150 Tg N/year (already substantially overshot).
global.context: NYC's nitrogen and phosphorus footprint is transmitted globally through its food system: importing produce, grain, meat, and dairy from farms that use synthetic fertilizer manufactured from mined phosphate rock (a finite resource concentrated in Morocco/Western Sahara) and fossil-fuel-derived nitrogen. A 2020 peer-reviewed 'community nitrogen footprint' methodology applied to Baltimore City (~19,000 metric tons N/year, ~30 kg N/capita/year, 73% from food production) is the closest published municipal-scale analog and shows this kind of analysis is feasible for a U.S. city; it has not, to my knowledge, been done for NYC. Separately, NYC exports its wastewater biosolids (roughly 500,000+ tons/year across all 14 WRRFs) largely to landfill and historically to out-of-state land application (Colorado, Florida, 1992-2010); each ton landfilled instead of land-applied represents phosphorus that is not being returned to agricultural soils, a lost-recovery issue tied to the finite global phosphate-rock reserve.
global.source: N-Print project (University of Virginia); Wang, Castellanos-Beltran et al. 'A community nitrogen footprint analysis of Baltimore City, Maryland' (IOPscience, 2020) as methodological analog

policyAnchors.name: 2023 CSO Consent Order Modification (DEC Case CO2-20110512-25, modifying CO2-20000107-8)
policyAnchors.relevance: Sets the binding citywide CSO reduction target (1.67 billion gallons/year by 2040) and green infrastructure spending commitment ($3.5B by 2045) that anchors the local-ecological CSO figure.
policyAnchors.status2026: Active and being reported on quarterly; a 2026 Q1 CSO quarterly report was found published by DEP, and DEP filed a Newtown Creek CSO Storage Tunnel FEIS/Notice of Completion in February 2026 and a Flushing Bay alternative storage-tunnel modification report in December 2025, indicating the consent order's major capital projects are actively moving through design/environmental review as of mid-2026.

policyAnchors.name: Sewage Pollution Right to Know Act (SPRTKA) enforcement
policyAnchors.relevance: A December 2023 NYS Supreme Court ruling found DEP had failed to meet SPRTKA's requirement to notify the public of CSO discharges within 4 hours; ongoing compliance affects how quickly residents learn of nitrogen/pathogen-bearing discharges before contact with waterways.
policyAnchors.status2026: Ruling issued December 2023 following litigation by Waterkeeper Alliance, Riverkeeper, NRDC and partners via the Pace Environmental Litigation Clinic; I could not confirm from available sources whether any appeal was filed or resolved by mid-2026 — flagged as unconfirmed.

policyAnchors.name: Long Island Sound Nitrogen TMDL (EPA-approved 2001)
policyAnchors.relevance: The binding regional target (58.5% aggregate reduction in human-generated nitrogen from a 1990 baseline) that NYC's East River WRRF upgrades were built to satisfy.
policyAnchors.status2026: NEIWPCC reports hypoxic area/volume in the Sound is trending down and NY/CT continue implementation alongside EPA's 2015 Nitrogen Reduction Strategy, but ecosystem-level targets (e.g., eelgrass extent) remain below goals — described as 'ongoing' rather than complete.

policyAnchors.name: 2010 Jamaica Bay Nitrogen Consent Agreement
policyAnchors.relevance: The specific $115M agreement ($100M WRRF nitrogen-control tech + $15M marsh restoration) that drove the Jamaica Bay WRRF nitrogen cuts and salt-marsh mitigation funding referenced in the local-ecological entry.
policyAnchors.status2026: Reported by Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers as substantially implemented, with the wetland mitigation fund created under the agreement noted as concluded in recent reporting; the 26th Ward carbon-addition facility (an additional, more recent nitrogen-control project) has separately been completed.

policyAnchors.name: NYS Clean Water, Clean Air and Green Jobs Environmental Bond Act (2022, $4.2B)
policyAnchors.relevance: A funding source explicitly eligible for CSO/stormwater and water-infrastructure projects (at least $200M for water infrastructure, at least $250M for stormwater/algal-bloom-related projects statewide), relevant to financing NYC's green infrastructure buildout.
policyAnchors.status2026: Passed by referendum in 2022; grant guideline documents were still being issued/revised into 2024, and the NY League of Conservation Voters published a 'three years on' status review — implementation is ongoing rather than complete.

actions: Sign up for NYC DEP's Sewage Pollution Right to Know Act discharge alerts before swimming, boating, or fishing in waterways like the Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay, or Jamaica Bay.

Comment during the Citywide (East River/Open Waters) and Jamaica Bay Long Term Control Plan public review processes (contact: ltcp@dep.nyc.gov) to push for faster green infrastructure buildout, given the city has already missed its 2015 and 2020 milestones.
Volunteer with Jamaica Bay Ecowatchers or the NY-NJ Harbor & Estuary Program on salt-marsh monitoring and restoration tied to the bay's nitrogen-loading history.

Support DEP's transition toward 100% beneficial reuse of biosolids (rather than landfilling) by following and commenting on DEP's Biosolids Management/Beneficial Use Plan solicitations, which also affects phosphorus recovery.

Track and testify at NYC Council's Committee on Environmental Protection, Resiliency and Waterfronts on CSO-reduction reporting and green infrastructure funding tied to the 2022 NYS Environmental Bond Act.
Reduce household use of high-phosphorus detergents/fertilizers, which still contribute to combined sewer and stormwater nutrient loads reaching CSO-affected waterways.
petalumaContrast: Petaluma's nitrogen & phosphorus story is groundwater nitrate near agricultural land and septic systems (most wells below the 10 mg/L drinking-water standard, with 4-7 mg/L hotspots near ag boundaries, scored level 20). NYC's is an engineered wastewater-and-CSO story roughly three orders of magnitude larger: 18 billion gallons/year of combined sewage through 398 outfalls citywide and 14 WRRFs whose historic point-source nitrogen loading required a $1B+ East River upgrade program and a separate 2010 Jamaica Bay consent agreement — there is essentially no diffuse agricultural-runoff analog in NYC's version of this dimension, and no groundwater-nitrate analog either, since NYC draws its water from upstate reservoirs rather than local wells.
dataGaps: A single, current, citywide total for nitrogen (and especially phosphorus) loading across all 14 WRRFs was not found; DEP/NYSDEC report by individual facility SPDES discharge monitoring reports (DMRs) of varying vintage, not a rolled-up citywide figure — NYC DEP's Bureau of Wastewater Treatment or NYSDEC's eDMR/EPA ECHO database would have the facility-level source data needed to build one.

No borough-aggregated CSO volume totals are published; DEP/DEC report by waterbody/watershed (Gowanus Canal, Newtown Creek, Flushing Bay, Jamaica Bay, Bronx River, etc.), which only partially maps to boroughs and sometimes spans two.

Current (2025/2026) biosolids destination and landfill-vs-beneficial-use percentages could not be confirmed; the figures found (roughly 69% landfill/31% beneficial use) appear to predate DEP's stated 2030 100%-diversion goal — DEP's current Biosolids Management/Beneficial Use Plan would have up-to-date figures.

No NYC-specific phosphorus loading or consumption-based phosphorus-footprint figure was found at all; this dimension is currently written almost entirely from the nitrogen side, which is defensible because nitrogen (not phosphorus) is the limiting, TMDL-regulated nutrient in NYC's marine/estuarine receiving waters, but a topic expert should confirm whether phosphorus deserves a more prominent, separately sourced sub-indicator.

The exact percentage of Staten Island's land area covered by the ~10,000-acre Bluebelt program (and therefore how much of the borough is truly free of combined-sewer/CSO exposure) was not found in a primary DEP source.

questionsForOrchestrator: Should the headline indicator be CSO annual volume (an infrastructure/public-health-adjacent proxy) or WRRF nitrogen loading (the more direct N/P planetary-boundary analog)? I scored and reported both under one dimension entry — confirm that's the right structure for cross-city comparability with Petaluma's single groundwater-nitrate indicator, or whether you want me to designate one as the sole headline.

Nitrogen is the TMDL-regulated, limiting nutrient in NYC's marine/estuarine receiving waters (Long Island Sound, Jamaica Bay), while phosphorus is more classically limiting in freshwater systems — I therefore treated phosphorus mostly through the global/biosolids lens rather than giving it an equal local sub-indicator. Confirm this weighting is consistent with how other agents (e.g. freshwater withdrawals, chemical pollution) are framing N vs. P, so the dimension doesn't read as incomplete relative to Petaluma's more P-inclusive framing.

The Jamaica Bay 'current ~18,000-20,000 lbs/day' nitrogen figure comes from community/NGO reporting (Rockaway Wave, NRDC), not a dated primary DEP monitoring report — if another agent or the orchestrator has access to NYSDEC's eDMR portal or EPA ECHO, a harder, dated number would meaningfully raise confidence on this dimension's headline value.
